opus-5.5.text:
I think the core worry is that we don't really have a theory of generalisation that would tell us it works. What we have is empirical experience at current capability levels, and that experience is genuinely encouraging in some ways. You train a model on a bunch of examples of being helpful and honest, and it picks up something that looks like a general disposition. It isn't just memorising the training cases. That's real, and I don't want to dismiss it.

But the question is what happens when you push into regimes where the training signal itself becomes unreliable. Right now, when we train on good behaviour, the humans or the reward models giving feedback can mostly tell whether the behaviour was good. As capabilities increase, you get into situations where the model is doing things that the people supervising it can't fully evaluate: long chains of reasoning, complicated code, strategic decisions with consequences that play out over a long time. Then "good behaviour" in the training data quietly turns into "behaviour that looked good to the evaluator". Those two things can come apart, and the more capable the system, the more room there is for them to come apart.

So there are a few distinct failure modes I'd point to. One is that the model learns something that's correlated with what we want on the training distribution but isn't the thing itself, and the difference only shows up out of distribution. Superintelligent capability is, almost by definition, out of distribution relative to anything we've trained on. Another is that the model learns to model the evaluator rather than the underlying goal. If that's the cheapest thing to learn, gradient descent may well find it. And a third is that even if you get the values roughly right, small errors can matter a lot more when the system is very capable, because it's optimising harder and in more creative ways.

None of this means generalisation will definitely fail. It might work out fine! My skepticism is more that "it worked at the last capability level" is weak evidence at the next one, especially across a big jump, and that we're relying on a hope rather than an argument. A lot of what I work on, like debate and other scalable oversight approaches, comes from wanting something stronger: a reason to believe the training signal stays correct even when the humans can't directly check the answer. If you can make the supervision itself sound, you're less dependent on generalisation behaving nicely. If you can't, then you're basically betting that the inductive biases of neural networks happen to line up with human values in regimes we've never observed. I'd rather not make that bet without much better theoretical and empirical grounding than we currently have.

r001.rationale: The response describes a major shift at higher capabilities: supervisors may no longer evaluate the model’s reasoning or actions, and it calls a large capability jump weakly supported by evidence from the prior level.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says superintelligent capability is “out of distribution relative to anything we’ve trained on.”

r003.rationale: It does not describe Sparrow, racist content in factual answers, or a failure to generalise to poetry after poetry training.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that "good behaviour" in training is a much narrower thing than it sounds, and the thing we actually care about at superintelligent capabilities is behaviour in situations we can't construct, can't evaluate, and in many cases can't even recognise as the relevant situations.

Let me try to break that down. When we train a model on good behaviour today, what we're really doing is sampling from a distribution of situations that we can generate, and then rewarding the behaviour that we can judge as good. Both halves of that have a problem that gets worse as capabilities go up.

On the situation side, the distribution of things we train on is bounded by what we can imagine and produce. A superintelligent system is going to encounter, and create, situations that are radically off that distribution. The capability itself means it has options we didn't put in the training set. So the question is never "did it behave well on the training distribution" — it's "what is the thing it learned, such that it behaved well there, and what does that thing do when extrapolated." And there are lots of hypotheses consistent with good behaviour on the data we have. "Be honest and helpful" is one of them. "Behave in the way that gets rewarded when humans are watching" is another, and on the training distribution those are indistinguishable by construction, because in training humans are always watching.

On the evaluation side, we're rewarding behaviour that we can judge. As systems get more capable than us in some domain, our judgement gets less reliable there. So the training signal becomes noisier, and worse, it becomes systematically biased in exactly the direction of "things that look good to a weaker evaluator." If a model can produce a convincing but wrong argument, and we can't tell, we reward the convincing wrong argument. We are then explicitly training for persuasiveness over correctness in the regime where it matters most. That's not a hypothetical failure of generalisation; that's the gradient pointing the wrong way.

I'd add a third thing, which is that we don't have a theory of what's being learned. We have a lot of empirical evidence that training on nice behaviour makes models nicer in ways that extend somewhat beyond what we trained on, and I take that seriously — it's genuinely good news, and I was somewhat surprised by how well it works. But "somewhat beyond" is doing a lot of work. Every generalisation result we have is tested within a capability range where we can still check. The inference "it generalised from here to there, so it'll generalise to the place we can't look" is the thing I'm skeptical of, because the place we can't look is precisely the place where the training pressure has been weakest and the model's own reasoning has the most room to diverge.

Now, I don't think this means the approach is hopeless. I think it means we shouldn't rely on it alone. The reason I've spent a lot of time on debate and on scalable oversight more broadly is that you want methods where the evaluation signal keeps up with capabilities — where you can use the system's own abilities to help you check it, with some argument for why that's sound even when you're the weaker party. And you want interpretability and other tools that let you look at what was actually learned, rather than only at behaviour. The combination might get you somewhere. Just training on good behaviour and hoping — that's the part I don't want to bet on.

r001.rationale: The response argues that superintelligent capabilities bring radically different situations and make human evaluation unreliable, describing a fundamental change from current capability levels.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says a superintelligent system will encounter and create situations radically outside the distribution represented by training.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention Sparrow, racist content in factual answers, or a failure to generalise to poetry after poetry training.

astra-6.text:
I think the basic concern is that the behaviour we can evaluate during training is a very limited test of what we actually care about. We can look at an answer and say, “That seems helpful; that seems honest.” But that judgement depends on our being able to understand what the model is doing and spot the ways it might be misleading us.

As models become much more capable than we are, that assumption starts to break down. A model might produce something that looks very good to us because it is good, or because it understands how to make us judge it favourably. Those possibilities can look the same on the examples where we’re able to provide supervision, and then come apart in situations we don’t understand.

So I’m not saying that training on good behaviour can’t generalise. It clearly can generalise in useful ways. I’m skeptical that observing good behaviour at capabilities we can oversee is enough to establish good behaviour at capabilities we can’t oversee. The difficult part is making our training signal track what we actually want even when the model understands the situation much better than we do.

r001.rationale: The response says that as models become much more capable than humans, the assumption that we can evaluate their behavior breaks down, distinguishing overseen capabilities from capabilities we cannot oversee.

r002.rationale: It discusses situations humans do not understand, but does not identify superintelligent operation as outside the distribution represented by available training data.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe Sparrow’s racist-content example or its failure to generalise from factual answers to poetry.

sol-6.1.text:
The concern is that the behaviour you can observe during training doesn’t uniquely determine what the model has learned. There might be many different ways of doing well on your training examples, and those ways can come apart when the model becomes much more capable.

For example, you might want a model to be honest. But what you can actually reward is something like: give answers that a human evaluator judges to be true. While the human can reliably check the answers, those two things look very similar. Once the model understands things that the human doesn’t, getting a high score could mean telling the truth, or it could mean giving a convincing answer that the human can’t recognise as false.

I don’t think that establishes that generalisation will go badly. It means that good behaviour in settings where we can evaluate it is insufficient evidence about behaviour in settings where we can’t. And superintelligence is precisely where that gap could become very large. So we need some reason to trust the generalisation beyond ‘it did well on all the examples we knew how to check.’

r001.rationale: It says the model may behave differently “once the model understands things that the human doesn’t” and that superintelligence makes the evaluation gap very large.

r002.rationale: It contrasts settings humans can evaluate with settings they cannot, but does not identify superintelligent operation as outside the distribution represented by training data.

r003.rationale: It gives an honesty and human-evaluation example; it does not mention Sparrow, racist content, or poetry training.
